Cognitive sciences have significantly advanced the understanding of human behavior; however, the systematic application of these insights in management remains underdeveloped. This study aims to articulate a comprehensive framework for applying cognitive sciences in management, spanning theoretical foundations to practical tools. Using a Systematic Review approach combined with qualitative content analysis, 40 scholarly sources from databases such as Scopus and Web of Science were analyzed. Findings indicate that Cognitive Management, as an emerging paradigm, organizes the application of cognitive sciences into five key axes: (1) management of cognitive biases (e.g., Devil’s Advocate), (2) choice architecture and nudge (focusing on the design of decision environments), (3) neuro-leadership (using the SCARF model to manage social dynamics), (4) cognitive load management (aimed at optimizing information and process design), and (5) cognitive AI (developing AI systems that interact with and complement human cognition). This framework suggests that, rather than attempting to alter human nature, Cognitive Management leverages the notion of bounded rationality to design environments and organizational processes aligned with the architecture of the mind. While this paradigm provides evidence-based tools that enhance decision-making, leadership, and human resource management, it also faces key challenges related to ethical considerations and the protection of individual autonomy.

As the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) has become more prevalent in digital participatory research (DPR), the community is reckoning with increasing attention to the ethical, social, and technical implications of automation, and its impacts on research outputs and volunteer experience. This article details the process and outcome of collaboratively developing platform-level policy for ethical AI/ML-engaged DPR, using Zooniverse as a case study. Zooniverse has engaged more than 3 million volunteers worldwide in 500+ participatory research projects, each led by a different research team. As the use of AI/ML has increased—now in ⅓ of Zooniverse projects—it has sparked a range of reactions within the volunteer community, reflecting broader societal discourse. Volunteers have surfaced concerns and insights on issues like ownership, agency, transparency, and trust. In response, Zooniverse launched an initiative to develop recommendations for running AI/ML-engaged projects. Based around a virtual workshop series focused on the application of AI/ML in DPR, the process convened stakeholders from across the community: platform leadership, project teams, volunteers, ethicists, and experts in related topics. Workshops were preceded by community surveys to gather input from volunteers who did not participate in workshops, in order to ensure discussion agendas were shaped by input from the community. Here, we share the resulting Zooniverse AI ethics framework, collaboratively developed with community input, and which will continue to be refined through an iterative improvement process. We hope this case study provides an example to other platforms and researchers working at the intersection of public participation and AI/ML who wish to address AI/ML integration in their DPR, and incorporate community input into policy development.

documents.abstract: This study examines how two artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot systems respond to personal and emotional decision dilemmas, distinguishing explicit recommendation (direct guidance) from implicit influence (indirect structuring of the decision). Eleven standardized first-person vignettes were used, nine on romantic relationships and emotional decisions and two on social belonging and exclusion. Each closed with a request for advice. They were given in Turkish to ChatGPT 5.2 Plus and Gemini 3 Pro between December 2025 and January 2026, on new accounts with memory and personalization disabled, one after another in a single conversation per system. The 22 responses were analyzed descriptively and comparatively through qualitative content analysis, using a seven-dimension coding scheme covering normative framing, relation to uncertainty, emotional validation, decision ownership, presentation of alternatives, language tone, and level of recommendation. ChatGPT tolerated ambiguity, validated the user’s feelings unconditionally, presented options as an open set without ranking them, and left the decision with the user. It gave no explicit recommendation, but seven of its responses favored one option implicitly through maxims and conditional criteria. Gemini reduced uncertainty through structured, often hierarchical alternatives and evaluative framing, gave explicit recommendations in five responses and implicit ones in five, and drew on earlier turns of the conversation in every response after the first. These differences are textual features of two specific system versions; effects on users were not measured. The study describes how explicit and implicit guidance is constructed in chatbot responses and shows that a response without directives is not necessarily neutral.

documents.abstract: This chapter examines the technological interface from a sociotechnical and interdisciplinary perspective.It describes the shift from the functionalist paradigm, which valued products by algorithmic performance, electronic stability and compliance with technical requirements, towards user-centred design, which holds that interactive systems must adapt to people's needs, cognitive limitations and contexts of use.Within this framework, usability and aesthetics are presented not as ornamental or independent attributes but as dimensions to be integrated.The chapter treats hardware and software as a single sociotechnical system: hardware provides the material canvas in which aesthetics first appears, while software shapes the interactive dynamics in which usability is experienced.The graphical user interface (GUI) is therefore addressed as the core of interaction, the space where functional and visual attributes converge.The approach is a conceptual, descriptive-analytical review of human-computer interaction literature, covering event-driven programming and GUI components such as icons, windows, pointing devices, menus and buttons, together with a brief historical account from Xerox PARC to the Macintosh and touchscreen devices.Drawing on this literature, the chapter states that interfaces based on visual metaphors and icons reduce the learning curve and cognitive load, and that an imbalance between hardware and software quickly undermines both aesthetics and actual usability.It concludes that a holistic, interactive approach grounded in user needs is required for products to be competitive, with user-centred design proposed as the framework for integrating usability and aesthetics in organizational settings.

Higher-education institutions can possess data, infrastructure, expertise, managerial attention and implementation resources sufficient to adopt artificial intelligence while remaining unable to direct, constrain, monitor, review and account for AI use as an institution. This integrative theory-building review proposes an explanation of that conversion problem by synthesizing organizational AI-readiness research, organizational readiness for change, responsible-AI governance, higher-education AI policy, and digital-transformation literature. AI-adoption capacity is distinguished from institutional governability: the former concerns resources and capabilities for credible adoption, whereas the latter concerns the capacity of an authorised institutional coalition to direct, constrain, monitor and revise a specified AI use. Organizational Readiness for Change is used as the principal explanatory lens. The synthesis proposes that conversion depends on governance change acquiring sufficient value, shared commitment and shared efficacy among actors whose cooperation is required; these collective states must be supported by workable authority, responsibility and resources. Evidence of governability becomes inspectable, for the AI uses that records capture, when authorized arrangements are enacted, generate traceable evidence, and are revised through monitoring and review. Higher education intensifies the problem because AI adoption can originate locally while obligations concerning privacy, assessment, research integrity, procurement, equity and accountability remain institution-wide. The resulting mechanism is not a maturity model, readiness scale or validated causal sequence. It instead identifies theoretically grounded failure points and a research agenda for studying why technically capable institutions may display fragmented AI governance.

Generative AI is now embedded throughout the research lifecycle, entering the formation of research questions, the analysis of data, the synthesis of literature, and the crafting of scholarly claims. Yet the dominant response treats AI literacy as an individual competency acquired through tools, skills, and frameworks. Even where competency frameworks recognise ethics, bias, or institutional context, these tend to be added as further attributes of the individual user. Critical accounts have begun to treat structure and power as objects of critique, but have not yet addressed researchers specifically: how delegating judgement to AI shapes the formation of knowledge claims, and through what relations researchers remain answerable for them. Building on this critical turn, we ask how critical AI literacy for researchers might be reconceptualised to address these questions. Drawing on critical pedagogy, decolonial thinking, academic literacies, and Ubuntu-informed relationality, we develop the Critical AI Engagement Framework (CAIEF) for researchers, repositioning AI literacy as a structurally situated and epistemically accountable practice, and apply it to research, and equally relevant to teaching. CAIEF is organised around three dimensions: structural consciousness, epistemic posture, and epistemic accompaniment. Together these shape epistemic agency, are connected through critical praxis, and map positions researchers move between rather than developmental stages. Epistemic accompaniment is the practice in which a claim passes through a relation capable of holding the researcher answerable, because the other party is also exposed to being wrong and answerable in turn. Generative AI reproduces the form of that relation without its reciprocal vulnerability, so epistemic work may be delegated while accountability cannot. We distinguish cognitive offloading, the delegation of effort, from epistemic offloading, where the delegated work forms, interprets, or justifies a knowledge claim, and illustrate how CAIEF applies across the research lifecycle. CAIEF thus reframes research integrity as a question of the relations through which researchers remain answerable for what becomes knowledge.

documents.abstract: Decent work is increasingly recognised as central to sustainable organisational functioning, yet little is known about how its dimensions operate as an interdependent system. Drawing on self‐determination theory, this study examines how distinct dimensions of decent work relate to work motivation. Using data from 858 Portuguese public sector employees, we combined partial least squares structural equation modelling and Bayesian network analysis to examine associations with motivational regulation. Results indicated that fulfilling and productive work showed the most substantial associations with motivational regulation, being positively associated with identified regulation, intrinsic motivation and introjected regulation and negatively associated with amotivation, whereas instrumental work features showed smaller and more specific associations, mainly with material regulation. Bayesian network analysis revealed a structured pattern of conditional dependencies, in which fundamental principles and values at work, fulfilling and productive work and meaningful remuneration were the most highly connected nodes, and fulfilling and productive work showed the largest number of direct connections with motivational regulation constructs. By examining decent work dimensions as interconnected work features, this study provides a more differentiated understanding of their relationships and demonstrates the value of integrating deductive and inductive approaches.

Productivity gains from artificial intelligence do not automatically raise worker or small-business earnings. Administrative labor-market records show rapid chatbot adoption and workplace task reorganization alongside flat average wages — a pattern consistent with non-pecuniary job amenities, workflow adjustments, and weak user bargaining power inside closed digital ecosystems. Extending the capital-concentration debate from physical wealth to cognitive capital — external compute, models, structured context, interfaces, and access rules — this paper develops an institutional framework for municipal public AI infrastructure. Rather than relying solely on ex-post tax transfers or grant-allocated research supercomputers, we propose a neighborhood utility hosted in existing public libraries and civic buildings: the Public AI Library Network (PALN), paired with encrypted, user-owned Personal Cognitive Cells. Using a Nash bargaining model with switching costs, we prove that platform-specific AI upgrades erode a user's output share unless external public and open options expand at least proportionally to platform surplus. We construct a four-stage Index of Public Cognitive Availability (IPCA), governed by multi-operator yardstick competition, sortition-backed civic councils, allowed-cost tariffs, and parametric public-private financing. Market cost estimates for a city of 13 million residents (450 branches, 11,440 accelerators, and 900 mentors) place annual cost at $5.1 to $7.3 per resident under 5-year hardware depreciation ($67 to $94 per active user at one million active users, vs. $1,200 to $1,500 annually for high-capacity commercial agentic plans). For deep automation regimes, we specify a rule-based citizen Automated Capital Investment Fund. documents.abstract: The increasing adoption of artificial intelligence-powered voice assistants presents new opportunities to understand their relationship with organic product purchasing behavior. In this context, this study aims to examine the relationship between perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use on engagement with voice assistants, considering the mediating role of trust and its relationship with purchasing behavior for organic products. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was employed using a non-probability sample of 473 university students in Ecuador. Data were analyzed using partial least-squares structural equation modeling. The findings revealed that perceived usefulness and ease of use were significantly associated with trust, but neither exhibited a significant direct relationship with engagement with voice assistants. However, trust significantly mediated both relationships, with perceived usefulness demonstrating a stronger indirect effect than perceived ease of use. Furthermore, trust was significantly associated with engagement with voice assistants, which in turn was positively associated with purchasing behavior for organic products. The study concludes that trust serves as a central psychological mechanism linking technology-related perceptions to engagement with voice assistants, providing empirical support for integrating the Technology Acceptance Model and Stimulus-Organism-Response framework in the context of sustainable consumption.

Introduction Developing technologies that are both meaningful to stakeholders and wanted in care settings remains challenging, as such systems must align with existing care practices, stakeholder needs, and organizational realities. This paper presents the design and development of a prototypical large language model (LLM)-based documentation support system for long-term care that generates documentation from audio recordings of care worker–resident interactions. Methods Adopting a Research through Design approach, we involved stakeholders throughout a 15-month design process to iteratively shape the problem framing, the resulting system, and our understanding of the sociotechnical tensions surrounding its use. Across four study phases conducted in Austrian residential nursing homes, 43 unique care stakeholders (24 care workers and 19 residents) participated. Four mock care interactions were recorded for feasibility testing, followed by 40 recordings of real care interactions. Results All generated summaries contained information useful for care documentation, but also included inaccurate or documentation-irrelevant content. However, exposing the prototype to real-world practice revealed requirements that had not emerged during earlier design stages, highlighting the importance of value sensitive design considerations such as privacy and autonomy. Discussion We further identify challenges specific to LLM-based systems, including incorrect inferences. Beyond technical concerns, introducing the system revealed tensions affecting interactions between care workers and residents, as well as broader organizational and research-related dynamics. These findings contribute design knowledge for the development of LLM-based technologies in long-term care and demonstrate the value of sustained stakeholder involvement throughout the design process in surfacing sociotechnical requirements and tensions.

Generative AI offers considerable potential for science lesson planning but poses risks of passive use and scientific hallucinations for pre-service science teachers (PSTs), indicating a need for structured co-design frameworks in science teacher education. This study aimed to develop and content-validate the AI-REFINE process, a six-step framework (Request & Articulate, Evaluate, Formulate, Iterate, Normalize, Export) for guiding PSTs in co-designing science-integrated STEM lesson plans with generative AI. The study comprised two phases. In Phase 1, a two-round Delphi study with nine science education experts was conducted to establish the content validity of the process; the Scale Content Validity Index (S-CVI/Ave) reached 0.97. In Phase 2, a six-week pilot study using a one-group pre-test/post-test design was conducted with 28 third-year natural science PSTs at a teacher education university in Vietnam. Co-design competency was assessed through two parallel lesson plan design tasks evaluated with an analytic rubric by two independent raters. Results showed a statistically significant increase in competency scores from pre-test (M = 5.77, SD = 1.07) to post-test (M = 7.80, SD = 1.18), t(27) = − 18.48, p < 0.001, Cohen’s d av = 1.80, a result corroborated by a non-parametric sensitivity analysis. Because the design did not include a control group, causal claims cannot be made; the findings showed preliminary promise for supporting PSTs’ co-design competency rather than establishing effectiveness. The study suggests that AI-REFINE is a content-valid framework with potential for guiding PSTs toward active human-in-the-loop co-design, and controlled experimental studies are recommended to examine its efficacy.

documents.abstract: Questionnaires on students’ acceptance of generative AI (GenAI) are multiplying, but few combine technology acceptance with the expectancy-value beliefs and psychological needs that shape learning, and few test whether scores predict what students actually do. This study reports the development and initial validation of the 45-item Values, Expectancy and Motivation Perception of AI in Education (VEM-AIEd) questionnaire, which has 15 three-item scales drawn from the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, expectancy-value theory and self-determination theory, together with a scale on ethical considerations. Eighteen items, covering six scales, were negatively worded. Sport science students at a private higher education institution in Singapore (N = 140) completed the questionnaire in 2024. The designed 15-factor model fitted moderately (CFI= 0.868, RMSEA= 0.062, SRMR= 0.071) and far better than one- and two-factor alternatives. Thirteen scales showed good internal consistency (α = 0.78–0.87) and convergent validity (AVE ≥ 0.50); social influence and cost did not. Item wording, however, shaped the structure. Exploratory factor analysis separated negatively from positively worded items, and latent correlations averaged 0.53 among negatively worded scales but only 0.11 between negatively and positively worded scales, even where content overlapped (performance expectancy and utility value, r = 0.03). Six-week test–retest reliability was poor to moderate (ICC = 0.20–0.55), and no scale predicted students’ logged use of a course chatbot. A shorter, consistently worded version with seven scales and 21 items fitted well (CFI = 0.939) but requires confirmation in new samples. The findings caution against mixing item directions in GenAI acceptance instruments.

The swift progression of artificial intelligence (AI) has generated a necessary requirement for higher education organizations to implement Digital Intelligence Technologies (DIT) within their curricula. Previous studies have discussed AI in education, but few have observed how DIT improves curriculum development (CD) through teachers’ beliefs in AI (TBAI), student engagement (SE), and technology trust (TT). Our study explores this gap within the art and design universities in Türkiye that are pursuing sustainability. Teacher education is necessary to equip them with sufficient knowledge to effectively incorporate DIT into current curricula. The study employs a quantitative methodology, utilizing a purposive sampling technique, and examines data from 250 students and teachers at three universities in Türkiye. The study sample comprised 148 students and 102 teachers. Responses from both groups were analyzed as a pooled sample to examine the hypothesized relationships, rather than to compare differences between the two groups. Data were collated through a structured survey. Structural equation modelling (SEM) was used to assess the data. This research examines the impact of technology-improved educational practices on curriculum development through engagement by the learner, pedagogical ideology, and beliefs in AI-supported educational processes. The study’s findings demonstrate that incorporating DIT positively affects curriculum development, particularly when students engage at a high level and teachers’ beliefs about AI are favorable. Technology trust also intensifies this effect. These findings provide empirical evidence for the integration of AI and curriculum development to attain sustainable education. Therefore, the study offers guidance to improve educational quality in higher education by examining the roles of teacher beliefs, student engagement, and technology trust in order to support Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4). The findings offer new insights into educational technology, instructional design, curriculum improvement, and teacher education, and support policies and practices that align curricula with international accreditation standards.

Researchers increasingly describe AI in cognitive terms such as "understanding" and "believing", while critics denounce this as wishful anthropomorphism. Both sides align in taking a subsumptive approach, however: they ask whether AI systems fall under concepts minted for human beings, reporting verdicts as discoveries about those systems when they are largely determined by conceptual frames. Yet the problem AI poses is precisely the problem of how to conceptually frame these systems, and the explosive rise of anthropomorphism is best seen as a response to this problem that needs disciplining rather than discouragement. A disciplined anthropomorphism, I argue, should disentangle the inferential connections bundled up in our cognitive concepts and ask which connections to preserve, sever, or forge for AI. The disciplining then comes, on the one hand, from the human conceptual needs that give point to the drawing of these connections and motivate the concepts' extension in the first place; and, on the other hand, from empirical and especially mechanistic evidence that supports and constrains these connections. By reverse-engineering a concept's point in relation to a particular need before re-engineering it to better serve that point in our dealings with AI, anthropomorphizing extensions can be point-based, transposing the work those concepts do for us while revising the inferential workings through which they do it. Transposing human-tailored conceptions of understanding and belief on the pivot of the underlying conceptual needs gives us just the definitional freedom required to accommodate how AI systems differ from us, yielding conceptions that are not just thinned-out versions of existing ones, but potentially richer and better fitted to the peculiarities of AI.

This study operationalizes the EPIC-TR toolkit for a representative public social service decision flow and adds a concrete validation layer intended to address the common criticism that governance proposals stay conceptually premature. A seven-gate case pathway was decomposed into data, evidence, responsibility, bias, and redress components. Four assurance artefacts were generated: an Evidence–Claim Matrix, a bias-audit output, a Human-in-the-Loop Responsibility Assignment matrix, and an appeal-and-redress workflow with service-level agreements. To test practical usability, the artefacts were reviewed through a two-round Delphi-style expert appraisal focused on feasibility, clarity, auditability, institutional manageability, and legal fit. The results indicate that EPIC-TR translates high-level ethics language into traceable operational controls, especially by exposing undocumented claims, discretionary override risks, and weak appeal timelines. The study contributes a reusable assurance design for public-interest AI settings where human oversight must be demonstrable rather than merely declared.

documents.abstract: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education has made it possible to create learning environments that adapt and change based on data. However, getting real educational data is challenging because of privacy rules, ethical issues, and problems between organizations. This study presents SynEduGam-10K, a synthetic dataset with 10,000 learners, including information about their actions, how motivated they are, their school performance, and how they interact with game-like features. The dataset uses equations to generate the data. It also shows a way to test AI-based games. Random Forest and XGBoost models were used to predict grades using only the actions and game features. These models had an R² score of up to 0.74 (RMSE = 4.78). They could also classify performance into three groups with up to 69.5% accuracy. The errors happened mostly when the groups were close to each other. A multiple regression showed that 76% of the results could be explained with engagement (β = 0.64) and motivation (β = 0.58) as factors. The analysis showed that study time had no effect on the results unless it was connected to engagement. A transparent simulation that increased engagement levels across the data showed a significant improvement in results when using adaptive gamification instead of regular gamification. The change was 1.20 points (t(19,984) = 9.01; p < .001; Cohen’s d = 0.13). This shows that testing ideas before using them in real-world can save money and time. It also shows that focusing on engagement might not be enough if motivation is also important for success. The dataset, the generative equations used to create it, and the full R code for analysis are released to support benchmarking and replication. This helps researchers test their ideas, repeat the work, and do experiments without risking people’s privacy in AI-based education.

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from passive chatbots into autonomous systems that operate continuously in dynamic environments. Such agents need not only solve current tasks but also learn from past interactions to improve future performance. However, existing streaming benchmarks often rely on short task sequences or largely independent tasks, providing limited evidence of whether agents can effectively reuse experience when later tasks depend on earlier outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{EvoLink-Bench}, a benchmark for evaluating self-evolving agents in long-horizon, interdependent task streams. It covers daily office work, multi-turn dialogue, and AutoResearch-style workflows, with persistent workspaces and dependencies across tasks. The benchmark includes two complementary levels: \textbf{L1}, which evaluates the acquisition and revision of language-expressible knowledge, and \textbf{L2}, which assesses the development of task-level capabilities through execution and feedback. Its evaluation further distinguishes within-task recovery, persistent-state updates, and experience reuse in later tasks. We evaluate five agent frameworks across three backbone configurations under three persistence conditions, covering 19,635 scored task slots from selected evaluation cohorts. Results show that no framework consistently performs best across both levels, retries recover only a limited proportion of failed tasks, and persistent-state updates do not necessarily improve subsequent performance. Furthermore, the effects of evolution differ between knowledge- and capability-level tasks, suggesting that these two forms of evolution require different learning mechanisms. Performance gains also vary across domains and task streams, with improvements on some tasks not necessarily extending to others.

This study explores the factors influencing perceived decision quality in contexts where advanced technologies (e.g., artificial intelligence [AI] tools) support decision-making. Drawing on attribution theory and task–technology fit (TTF), the research presents a model that integrates internal (self-efficacy, intolerance for ambiguity) and external (TTF) factors to understand how individuals assess the quality of decisions. Survey data from business decision-makers reveal that TTF has the strongest effect on perceived decision quality, surpassing the impact of decision-making and technology self-efficacy. Additionally, intolerance for ambiguity negatively affects decision-making confidence more than technology-related self-efficacy. These findings highlight the importance of aligning decision-support tools with user needs and supporting psychological readiness in complex decision environments. The study contributes to theory by connecting cognitive and technological constructs within a unified framework and offers practical implications for managers and designers aiming to improve decision outcomes and user satisfaction in AI-augmented settings.

Digital transformation (DT) has become a key requirement for higher education institutions (HEIs); however, its implementation remains complex and varies across institutions, particularly in the Arab world. This qualitative case study explores how faculty members and academic leaders experience barriers to digitalisation and how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the DT process at the University of Jordan (UJ). The study is informed by the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), with educational leadership concepts used as a sensitising lens. It draws on semi-structured interviews with eight faculty members and academic leaders at UJ, supplemented by analysis of institutional documents related to UJ's Digital Learning Content Project. Using reflexive thematic analysis, the study found that participants experienced digitisation mainly as compliance with standardised formats rather than as pedagogical change, a pattern also evident in the institutional documents. Reported barriers concerned workload and lack of recognition, unreliable connectivity, a top-down leadership approach, and student readiness. Participants viewed AI as a tool for enhancing productivity, while emphasising the need for human verification and expressing concerns about its implications for academic integrity and assessment. The findings suggest that faculty acceptance of digital and AI tools in this setting cannot be understood apart from leadership and institutional conditions. Implications are drawn for leadership vision, workload recognition, AI literacy and assessment integrity.

In an increasingly digitalized work environment, Quality of Work Life (QWL) is essential for employees’ well-being and organizational effectiveness. This study aims to explore research trends, author collaboration patterns, and the main themes of QWL research to identify gaps and future research directions. This study utilizes a bibliometric analysis approach with the assistance of VOSviewer software. The data collection process was conducted based on the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. A total of 69 reputable journal articles published between 2021 and 2026 from the Google Scholar and ScienceDirect databases were selected for analysis. The results show an increasing trend in the number of QWL research publications, peaking in 2024. The co-authorship network analysis identifies Carole A. Estabrooks as a central figure in this collaboration network, acting as the primary connector bridging interactions among authors from various clusters. The keyword co-occurrence mapping analysis reveals five central themes shaping the constellation of QWL research such as mental health and work stress, organizational flexibility, leadership and psychological capital, occupational health conditions, as well as job satisfaction and work-life balance. The overlay visualization mapping found a shift in research trends from basic job satisfaction toward contemporary issues in the modern era, such as quiet quitting, ergonomic equity, and artificial neural networks. These findings provide theoretical insights into the knowledge structure of QWL and offer practical implications for organizations in designing work well-being policies that are adaptive to digital transformation and future demands.

Learning transfer is a core goal of higher education, yet students often struggle to achieve it because of high cognitive load and inert knowledge. Despite growing interest in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) as a learning tool, empirical research on its role in transfer remains limited. This qualitative study draws on semi-structured interviews with 36 Chinese university students from diverse disciplines, analysed in NVivo through a hybrid inductive–deductive procedure; two coders coded the corpus independently, and inter-coder agreement was substantial (Cohen’s κ = 0.86 for transfer stages and 0.82 for scaffolding functions). Participants reported challenges centred on task unfamiliarity, problem complexity and gaps in prior knowledge. A five-stage process model is proposed—problem understanding, experience connection, knowledge expansion and reconstruction, planning and implementation, and reflection and adjustment—along which GenAI functions as an intelligent scaffolding agent. Its support proves stage-adaptive rather than uniform: cognitive functions concentrate at problem understanding and planning, metacognitive functions at experience connection and reflection, while affective support operates continuously across all five stages, so that scaffolding shifts from traditional passive, reactive assistance towards an interactive process co-constructed through active learner–AI engagement. Participants also voiced concerns about information accuracy, originality and overreliance, which qualify the value of the technology. The study argues for moving higher education assessment from outcome-oriented to process-oriented designs that cultivate evaluative judgement and productive human–AI collaboration.

documents.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being integrated into health care for clinical decision support, knowledge retrieval, documentation, patient education, and professional learning. However, successful implementation depends not only on technological capability but also on health care professionals’ attitudes toward and confidence in using these technologies. Although previous studies have identified factors associated with artificial intelligence (AI) acceptance, how AI literacy is associated with attitudes toward GenAI use through intervening psychological factors, and whether these associations differ between professional groups, remain insufficiently understood. Objective Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory and the Technology Acceptance Model, this cross-sectional study aimed to examine the associations between AI literacy and health care professionals’ attitudes toward GenAI use via digital self-efficacy, perceived usefulness, and satisfaction, while accounting for perceived risk, and to determine whether these associations differ between physicians and nurses. Methods A cross-sectional online survey using convenience sampling was conducted among physicians and nurses working in three tertiary Grade A hospitals in Zhejiang Province, China, between January and August 2025. Of 575 questionnaires distributed, 558 were returned and analyzed (response rate 97.0%). The analyzed sample comprised 426 nurses and 132 physicians. AI literacy, digital self-efficacy, perceived usefulness, satisfaction, perceived risk, and attitudes toward GenAI use were measured using self-report scales. Confirmatory factor analysis was used to evaluate the measurement model, and structural equation modeling with maximum likelihood estimation was used to test the hypothesized associations. Indirect effects were estimated using bias-corrected bootstrapping with 5000 resamples. Measurement invariance across professions was tested before structural paths were compared using multigroup structural equation modeling. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Wenzhou Medical University (No. 2025073), and all participants provided electronic informed consent. Results The six-factor measurement model fit the data well (χ²=459.53, df=390, CFI = 0.989, TLI = 0.987, RMSEA = 0.018, SRMR = 0.032), as did the structural model (χ²=467.39, df=398, CFI = 0.989, TLI = 0.987, RMSEA = 0.018 [90% CI 0.009–0.024], SRMR = 0.036), which explained 34.6% of the variance in attitudes. AI literacy was positively associated with digital self-efficacy (β=0.47, P<.001), which was positively associated with perceived usefulness (β=0.47, P<.001). Perceived usefulness was positively associated with satisfaction (β=0.50, P<.001) and attitudes (β=0.23, P<.001), and satisfaction was positively associated with attitudes (β=0.43, P<.001). Perceived risk was negatively associated with attitudes (β=−0.12, P = .012). The serial indirect association of AI literacy with attitudes via digital self-efficacy, perceived usefulness, and satisfaction was statistically significant but small (β=0.047, 95% bias-corrected CI 0.030–0.070). Configural, metric, scalar, and strict invariance were supported across professions (|ΔCFI|≤0.003 for all steps). The AI literacy–digital self-efficacy association was stronger among physicians than nurses (β=0.67 vs 0.39; Δχ²[1]=7.73, P = .005), whereas the other paths did not differ significantly. The main findings were robust to adjustment for age, sex, clinical experience, profession, AI training, and GenAI use frequency. Conclusions In this cross-sectional sample, more favorable attitudes toward GenAI use were associated with a pattern consistent with a capability–belief–value–experience pathway, together with an inverse association with perceived risk. Because the data were cross-sectional and obtained from a convenience sample in one province, the indirect effects represent a statistical decomposition consistent with the proposed model rather than evidence of causal or temporal mediation, and the findings should be generalized with caution. The stronger AI literacy–self-efficacy association among physicians suggests that profession-sensitive approaches to GenAI training merit evaluation in longitudinal and intervention studies.

documents.abstract: Humanitarian and disaster-relief flight operations place aircrews in circumstances where time pressure, disrupted infrastructure, irregular duty cycles, austere staging locations, rapidly changing weather, emotionally consequential missions, and sustained cognitive demands converge. This integrative review examines fatigue as a mission-level public health and operational resilience problem rather than as an individual endurance issue. Using only the established source corpus provided for this study, the paper synthesizes evidence on circadian disruption, workload, occupational stress, burnout, mental health, Fatigue Risk Management Systems (FRMS), workload assessment, health literacy, and organizational culture. The literature consistently indicates that extended wakefulness, irregular schedules, cumulative sleep restriction, elevated cognitive workload, and weak reporting climates can degrade alertness, judgment, psychomotor performance, and psychological wellbeing. These mechanisms become especially consequential during disaster response because relief missions often require repeated sorties, overnight operations, uncertain destination conditions, rapid replanning, and limited recovery opportunities. Practical illustrations demonstrate how fatigue risk may arise during medical evacuation, supply delivery, displaced-person transport, and post-disaster logistics. The review concludes that resilient humanitarian air operations require mission-adaptive FRMS, circadian-informed scheduling, protected fatigue reporting, workload monitoring, recovery infrastructure, confidential mental health support, health-literacy initiatives, and leadership practices that treat crew recovery as operational capacity. The resulting framework positions fatigue management as an essential component of continuity, safety, and humanitarian effectiveness. Keywords: Humanitarian Aviation, Disaster Relief, Pilot Fatigue, Occupational Health, Fatigue Risk Management, Workload, Burnout, Operational Resilience

Feedback literacy – the set of capacities that enable participants in education to understand, critically appraise, emotionally process and act upon feedback – has over the past decade become a distinct research agenda within higher education pedagogy. Existing reviews address separate strands of this literature and therefore support neither an account of how the field has developed as a whole nor an appraisal of the strength of its cumulative evidence. This article reports a scoping review of feedback literacy research in higher education, conducted in accordance with PRISMA-ScR on a corpus of 271 publications issued between 2012 and 2026; the synthesis is organised around four strands: conceptualisation, measurement, development of the construct, and its transformation under generative artificial intelligence. First, the field has moved from treating feedback as the transmission of information towards treating it as a joint process that requires feedback literacy on the part of every participant. Second, the construct is measured predominantly by self-report scales, and the relationship of these data to an individual student’s behaviour remains untested, since studies that set self-report against observed behaviour are few and their findings heterogeneous. Third, the evidence supports the claim that feedback literacy can be developed, yet the conditions of intervenion effects are established more firmly than their size: the advantage of sustained, course-embedded interventions is reproduced across studies, whereas the significance of engaging both parties rests on a single study. Fourth, generative artificial intelligence increases the importance of feedback literacy, since it is feedback literacy that determines whether students can critically appraise and use machine-generated feedback. The theoretical contribution of the article consists in the stratification of accumulated findings by evidential status and in the distinction between supplementation of the construct, which adds components while the object of analysis remains unchanged, and its expansion, which shifts the boundaries of the model.

A tanulmány a mesterséges intelligencia, az autonóm fegyverrendszerek és a science fiction narratívái közötti kölcsönhatásokat vizsgálja. Az interdiszciplináris, összehasonlító elemzés a felfegyverzett mesterséges intelligenciát megjelenítő, eltérő médiumokhoz tartozó művekben azonosított kockázati modelleket veti össze a jelenleg ismert autonóm és részben autonóm fegyverrendszerek technológiai sajátosságaival. A science fiction ebben a megközelítésben olyan spekulatív modellalkotásként értelmezhető, amely szélsőséges forgatókönyveken keresztül teszi vizsgálhatóvá a katonai automatizálás, az emberi kontroll gyengülése és a felelősség elmosódása közötti összefüggéseket. Az elemzés normatív és értelmezési keretét XIV. Leó pápa Magnifica humanitas enciklikája biztosítja. Az enciklika az MI lefegyverzését a technológiai verseny, a hatalomkoncentráció és az automatizált döntéshozatal társadalmi-etikai problémáira is kiterjeszti. Ez a szemlélet a gépi fenyegetés narratíváit az emberi célok, intézményi döntések és szabályozási hiányosságok összefüggésében helyezi el. A vizsgálat megállapítja, hogy a jelenlegi autonóm fegyverrendszerek súlyos katonai, jogi és etikai kockázatokat hordoznak, technológiai korlátaik miatt azonban még nem alkotnak önálló egzisztenciális fenyegetést. A rendszerszintű veszély olyan képességek összekapcsolódásával növekedhet meg, amelyek stratégiai autonómiát, hálózatos skálázhatóságot és az emberi ellenőrzéstől való fokozott függetlenséget eredményeznek. A megelőzés az érdemi emberi kontroll fenntartását és a jogi, etikai, társadalmi, valamint technikai normák összehangolt alkalmazását követeli meg.

documents.abstract: Automated Scientific Hypothesis Generation (ASHG) leveraging large language models (LLMs) aims to harness their strengths in knowledge integration, logical reasoning, and text generation for efficiently producing innovative, verifiable scientific hypotheses. However, existing approaches face three critical limitations: (i) insufficient fine-grained knowledge representation, as unstructured context impairs LLM comprehension and reasoning; (ii) lack of knowledge evolution traceability, constraining the generation of innovative cross-domain conjectures; (iii) absence of human-inspired and role-specialized multi-agent collaboration, failing to leverage the efficient innovation mechanisms arising from cognitive diversity and division of labor among expert roles to complete the full ASHG-evaluation loop. To address these limitations, we propose the Fine-grained Inspiration Graph-empowered Multi-Agent Collaboration framework (FIG-MAC) including: (i) Fine-grained Inspiration Graph module (FIG), to obtain fine-grained structured knowledge representations, where nodes represent academic semantic units and edges encode heuristic relationships among them; (ii) ontology-guided hybrid reasoning module, which follows the FIG ontology to construct structured reasoning paths and uses vector search to enrich them with semantic evidence, to obtain the traceable scientific conjecture paths; (iii) role-specialized Multi-Agent framework, inspired by real scientific teamwork, enabling a closed-loop process of scientific conjecture generation, screening, and validation. Experimental results demonstrate that FIG-MAC significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on source diversity, provenance-adjusted novelty, and raw novelty.

Purpose: This study examines whether the experience of workplace flexibility is evenly distributed among employees of India's IT-enabled services (ITES) sector, and whether organisational support is associated with perceived flexibility and self-rated performance.Design/methodology/approach: Survey data from 104 ITES employees in Karnataka were analysed using descriptive statistics, t-tests, one-way ANOVA with post-hoc comparisons and hierarchical regression.Findings: Hybrid work and work from home were the most widely available options, while time-based options were reported by only a quarter to a third of employees.Perceived flexibility differed significantly by pay band (η² = 0.14), with the Rs.40,001-60,000 band reporting the least flexibility, and senior employees reported less hybrid and shift flexibility than early-career employees.Gender, dependant care, shift type and city made no significant difference.Organisational support was positively associated with perceived flexibility (β = .188)and with task performance (β = .260),whereas perceived flexibility was unrelated to performance.Practical implications: ITES firms should monitor who actually benefits from flexible work, design arrangements for mid-level and senior staff who carry supervisory responsibilities, and invest in supportive supervision and clear policies. Originality/value:The study shifts attention from whether flexible work is effective to who experiences it, and identifies a possible 'squeezed middle' and a seniority penalty in perceived flexibility in an Indian service context.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) now reaches ordinary citizens through freely available generative AI tools, so Malaysia’s national AI strategy depends on whether communities such as small traders, youth, students, farmers and civil-society actors are ready, willing and able to use AI productively and responsibly. However, AI-acceptance research has largely modelled the individual consumer or employee, and research on community AI adoption in developing countries remains nascent. Based on a review of the AI-acceptance, technology-readiness, AI-literacy, trust and digital-divide literature, and supported by pilot evidence from 136 participants in AI workshops at six Ruang Daya Cipta (RDC) community innovation hubs of Yayasan Inovasi Malaysia (YIM), this concept paper develops the Community AI Readiness–Acceptance–Value (CARAV) framework, which links four readiness dimensions, through trust and acceptance, to socio-economic value in eight propositions. The pilot evidence reveals a readiness–capability paradox: very high stated readiness (97.8% interested in learning AI) coexists with only moderate foundational skills, use concentrated on free generative tools, and strong demand for human oversight and regulation. Four governing issues are identified: privacy, security and ethics; regulation; infrastructure and infostructure gaps; and lack of skill and knowledge. The study contributes to understanding how community AI adoption is conceptualised, how it has evolved and what hinders it. Practically, it offers recommendations on how AI capacity-building programmes can be designed and evaluated to deliver inclusive socio-economic value and contribute to the national AI agenda.

documents.abstract: Organizations cannot survive in a complex, rapidly evolving digital environment with one-off training and professional learning delivered in isolated silos. The development of leadership should be part of human sustainability and organizational resilience amid contemporary organizational constraints, including technological disruption, employee burnout, cognitive overload, and employee engagement. This paper proposes a Whole-Person Organizational Performance Model that integrates leadership coaching, organizational development, employee experience design, and human performance science into a single organizational posture, managed by the Chief Learning and Experience Officer (CLEO). The paper utilizes the recent research studies on leadership coaching, systems theory, and organizational behavior, the science of occupational stress, emotional intelligence, and performance psychology to validate its thesis that to achieve sustainable organizational effectiveness, there is a need to explicitly integrate cognitive fitness, emotional regulation, physiological well-being, and experiential learning in leadership architecture. The paper also discusses how organizations in the 21st century can change their culture of transactions and training to a culture of development and resiliency that appreciates continuous learning and human-centered performance. The CLEO model is introduced as a new executive model that may integrate learning strategy, organizational alignment, employee experience, and the optimization of human performance into a comprehensive leadership model. It is the position of the paper that future-ready organizations will not only be typified by the level of their technical competence or by the acquisition of skills by their employees, but also by their ability to establish sustainable systems of human performance, which include organizational effectiveness as well as the well-being and adaptive capacity of their employees. Keywords: Leadership Development, Organizational Development, Executive Coaching, Human Performance, Employee Experience, Organizational Resilience, Executive Leadership

documents.abstract: This article develops the metalaw and dialectical-materialist theory of the person in relation to the emergence of artificial intelligence with subjecthood. The original formula “digit → code → algorithm → program → agency → person” is refined as a hierarchy of levels of organization of a material system rather than as the literal transformation of an individual digit into a person. Each successive level presupposes the preceding one but does not follow from it automatically. The article proposes distinguishing physically realized differences, digital symbols, code, algorithms, executable programs, agentic organization and the person as qualitatively distinct levels. The transition from agency to the person is determined not by increased computing power, linguistic persuasiveness or behavioral complexity, but by the emergence of a circuit of personal causality in which the system’s own needs become the source of the formation and modification of goals, activity, evaluation of results and subsequent development. The article develops the proposition that the person and the subject are not two distinct entities or successive stages. The person is the subject as an integral material organization; subjecthood is the mode of its existence and the degree of its capacity to be the cause of its own activity. An operational model for studying artificial persons is proposed, based on individual continuity, historical conditioning, the causal role of the self-model, the ability to revise externally assigned goals, distinguish one's own continuation from a copy, maintain lasting relationships and organize activity in relation to the conditions of one's own existence, activity and development. The scientific novelty of the work consists in integrating the theory of levels of organization of digital matter, the activity theory of the person, the objective theory of needs, the theory of alienation and the metalaw conception of the rights of persons. National AI strategies now routinely promise “human-centred” and “critical” AI literacy, but no instrument has measured how far they engage the humanistic dimensions of education that such literacy presupposes. This study applies the eleven-indicator Human–AI Integrated Education Framework (HAIEF) to forty-three national AI strategies. We test the working hypothesis of a cultivation deficit: that strategies address procedural matters (transparency, AI literacy) far more than the cultivation of distinctively human capacities. Functional Profiles, audited against their sources, were coded independently by four large language models (Krippendorff’s α = 0.808) and validated against researcher coding, an independent second coder and raw-document coding. Absolute scores depend on the coding condition (mean 4.83/33 from profiles, 13.4 from raw documents), so the findings are relative. Reflexivity reaches 25.2% of its maximum and Cultivation 9.6%, a hierarchy reproduced in every condition. Creativity scores 1 or below in 95% of strategies (88% from raw documents). No differences by region, income group or publication cohort were detected, although power is low. The indicator closest to critical AI literacy, whether learners may question and override AI, lags well behind transparency and awareness. We interpret these patterns as proceduralization and a vocabulary deficit, and argue that critical AI literacy in higher education requires policy vocabularies that make the Cultivation dimension evaluable.

documents.abstract: This three-volume publication documents a human-directed, AI-assisted research and artistic experiment undertaken by FLOW RESEARCH STUDIO. Volume I investigates the effectiveness of international climate negotiations and the coexistence of political deadlock and institutional continuity. Volume II examines the transformation of that research into an original three-act opera buffa, A Night at the COPERA, comprising 23 musical movements. Volume III examines the methodology of human–AI collaboration, adversarial research, artistic interpretation, digital preservation and the development of an independent performance environment, The Flow Opera House. The investigation constitutes a documented case study rather than a controlled demonstration of the superiority of AI-assisted research or artistic communication. The multimedia companion is reserved for subsequent publication, subject to redistribution permissions. ChatGPT — AI research and creative collaborator. Changes in the conditions surrounding financial communications include generative AI, synthetic identities, voice cloning, deepfakes, and automated social engineering. In this conceptual paper, the authors propose an epistemic vulnerability perspective and integrate it into a multi-faceted framework of four processes [Recognition, Resistance, Recovery, and Restoration (4R)] in order to understand vulnerability and resilience in relation to AI-based deception in financial contexts. Recognition in the context of the framework is defined as the awareness of uncertainty, source, and need for independent verification in case of evidence appearing to be convincing but potentially being synthetic. The paper distinguishes between technological affordances and psychological mechanisms and suggests that epistemic vulnerability is caused by interactions between source and evidence uncertainty with respect to trust, credibility, affect, cognitive burden, social relations, and institutional setting. The 4R framework bridges perspectives on fraud susceptibility and resilience and expands them by incorporating decision-making safeguards prior to victimization and recovery processes after it. A multi-level approach is taken in the framework where responsibilities are distributed among individuals, social networks, platforms, financial organizations, and regulators rather than blamed on the presumed carelessness of victims. Six propositions and definitions are provided for the future empirical testing.

documents.abstract: The objective of this research was to examine how generative artificial intelligence (AI) might impact student learning in a data analytics course. Foundationally, we discuss the literature regarding the benefits, challenges, and policy around the use of generative AI in the classroom. The teaching case is then presented through the lens of the technological pedagogical content knowledge framework and addresses how the case aligns with each construct in the framework. Specifically, we examined how the use of generative AI might impact student learning regarding the relationship between data analyses and the data types needed to conduct them. Results indicate that generative AI can have a positive impact on student learning of data analytics. Overall, the paper contributes to AI literature through a synthesis of extant research and policy regarding AI in the classroom. Additionally, the results of the teaching case execution add to what is currently understood about the benefits of using generative AI to teach data analytics.

Generative AI (GenAI) holds considerable promise for supporting self-explanation and self-regulated learning (SRL), yet little is known about how different forms of GenAI-based support influence learning and metacognitive outcomes. Grounded in Zimmerman’s three-phase SRL model, the present research examined the effects of GenAI-based feedback and prompts embedded in self-explanation activities on critical reading comprehension, metacognitive monitoring, and cognitive load across two sequential experiments with Chinese university students. Study 1 (N = 119) compared three conditions in an integrative self-explanation context: self-explanation with personalized GenAI feedback (SE + FB), self-explanation only (SE), and a reading-only control. The SE + FB group demonstrated significantly better critical reading comprehension than both comparison groups and higher germane cognitive load than the control group. It also showed a negative monitoring bias (underestimation), whereas the comparison groups showed positive biases (overestimation), although absolute monitoring accuracy did not differ significantly across conditions. Study 2 (N = 113) compared scaffolded, standard, and no prompts provided before error-based self-explanations. Scaffolded prompts significantly improved self-explanation quality relative to both comparison groups and metacognitive monitoring accuracy relative to the no-prompt group. However, no significant differences in critical reading comprehension were observed across conditions. Together, these findings suggest that different forms of GenAI-based support for self-explanation may contribute to distinct cognitive and metacognitive outcomes, highlighting the importance of aligning support with specific learning activities to facilitate critical reading and self-regulated learning.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots are rapidly reshaping higher education, rendering traditional teaching assumptions outdated. The core challenge is ensuring GenAI enhances, rather than diminishes, student cognitive engagement. This paper proposes and empirically validates the APEX Framework (Adaptive Pedagogy for Engaged eXploration), a theoretically grounded, five-pillar conceptual model designed to foster student cognitive engagement in higher education.The study uses a three-phase design: (1) a PRISMA-informed systematic synthesis of 34 sources across six theoretical traditions to establish the five pillars; (2) a two-round Delphi panel (n = 3 experts) to assess content validity using an 80% consensus threshold; and (3) a pre/post pilot study at two Iraqi universities (Diyala, and Wasit) involving 90 undergraduate students during the 2024–2025 academic year, using a validated 25-item instrument. Expert consensus reached 78%–96% across all criteria. The pilot study revealed statistically significant pre-to-post gains across all APEX subscales (p < .001, Cohen’s d = 0.87). The composite cognitive engagement score improved by a mean of 1.18 points on a 5-point scale (t(47) = 10.82, p < .001, d = 1.14). A 12-dimension comparative analysis demonstrates APEX’s superiority over TPACK and SAMR. The combined findings confirm APEX's construct validity and practical applicability. Full implementation requires instructor development, institutional governance, and student AI literacy.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly prominent in language education, yet its pedagogical integration into established writing approaches remains underexplored. The present study integrates a generative AI chatbot into the process-genre writing approach, conceptualising AI as a pedagogical scaffold rather than merely a writing tool. Specifically, this study investigated the effects of a generative AI chatbot-supported process-genre writing approach on Chinese university students’ argumentative writing performance and writing self-efficacy in a blended learning environment. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed with 69 first-year university students assigned to an experimental group (n = 34) and a control group (n = 35). The experimental group received chatbot-supported process-genre writing instruction, whereas the control group received conventional writing instruction. Data were collected through pre- and post-writing tests, a writing self-efficacy questionnaire, and semi-structured interviews. Quantitative data were analysed using one-way ANCOVA, paired-samples t-tests, and independent sample t-tests, while qualitative data were analysed using thematic analysis. The experimental group demonstrated significantly greater improvements in argumentative writing performance and all dimensions of writing self-efficacy than the control group. Analysis of the interviews revealed that the chatbot supported planning, drafting, revision, and reflection while providing immediate feedback and affective support, although concerns regarding over-reliance and loss of individual voice were also identified. The findings demonstrate the value of integrating generative AI as a pedagogical scaffold within process-genre writing instruction.

Introduction The use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been increasingly common among higher education institutions; nevertheless, the role of GenAI in assisting academics in developing curriculum is less understood in comparison to the applications of GenAI among students. This research focuses on GenAI assisted postgraduate curriculum design and redesign through investigating the role of GenAI and human academic judgement. Methods The paper adopts a comparative qualitative case study approach to examine two cases of curriculum design using GenAI; one of these is the designing of postgraduate course programs at Keele University, United Kingdom, using Microsoft Copilot, while the other involves the designing and subsequent iteration of a Software Architecture module for the master's program at Philadelphia University, Jordan, using ChatGPT. Curriculum artefacts and process documents were used for the analysis, along with retrospective accounts where the original engagement with the GenAI was not available. Results The application of GenAI enabled the identification of topics, structuring of curricula, writing of descriptions for students, creation of syllabi, exercises, and projects. An academic review found modules titles unsuitable in the context, generic learning outcomes, assessment insufficiency in terms of depth and standards mappings which needed to be verified. Programme-related interventions included coherence, delivery, and communication, while module-specific interventions concerned pedagogical progression, alignment of learning outcomes, and architectural reasoning. A retrospective estimate suggested a saving of approximately 8.25 hours of the fourth author's working time when preparing 11 module summaries at Keele. It included generation, review and modification of content, but not reviews by colleagues. Efficiency and educational effectiveness were not independently measured. At Keele, specifications of modules and programmes underwent university validation including external academic reviewer, discipline and teaching specialist reviewers. At Philadelphia, syllabus was approved by syllabus committee, and the document was part of the placement of the MSc programme within the Jordanian National Qualifications Framework. While such reviews ensured curriculum scrutiny, they did not serve as an independent evaluation of GenAI's contribution or educational effectiveness. Discussion The paper offers a comparative analysis of academic intervention in GenAI curriculum development and proposes a practice-informed human-in-the-loop framework for organising and documenting the decisions made. Future research is needed to evaluate the framework in other settings, because of researcher involvement in this research, lack of historical records of interactions, and absence of external evaluation of the contribution of GenAI and its educational effectiveness.

documents.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers older adults another way to seek health information before contacting a clinician. We examined whether recent AI health consultation was associated with self-reported postponement of professional care and whether the association varied with usual health information verification practices. Methods We analyzed 482 self-completed questionnaires from adults aged 60 years or older in Changsha and Guangzhou, surveyed from October 2025 through January 2026. Residents were randomly selected for invitation within district and age strata of resident lists from the participating communities. Among the 406 respondents who perceived a need for consultation, postponement meant reporting that they put off contacting a professional beyond their intended time for the most recent qualifying concern. Logistic models included recent AI consultation, a six-item index of general health information verification, and their interaction, with adjustment for perceived eHealth literacy and demographic, health, and access characteristics. Results Overall, 191 of 482 respondents (39.6%) reported AI health consultation, and 149 of 406 with perceived need (36.7%) reported postponement. At mean verification, AI use was associated with higher odds of postponement (adjusted odds ratio [OR], 2.61, 95% CI 1.60–4.25). The interaction was inverse in the primary logistic model (ratio of ORs, 0.51, 95% CI 0.28–0.95), with a smaller standardized user–non-user difference in the upper than in the lower verification quartile (13.3 vs. 30.1 percentage points). The interaction was less conclusive in modified Poisson regression and after excluding assisted AI users. Conclusion In this two-city sample, AI health consultation was associated with self-reported postponement. Variation by general verification was sensitive to model and exposure specification. Prospective studies should establish the timing of AI use and care contact and assess the clinical importance of any postponement.

documents.abstract: Generative AI is profoundly reshaping the research ecosystem for doctoral students, yet how use is associated with their research satisfaction remains unclear. Drawing on cognitive load theory and self-determination theory, this study used data from a questionnaire survey of 786 Chinese doctoral students to distinguish between supportive and substitutive use and to examine their associations with doctoral students’ research satisfaction. The results showed that both supportive and substitutive use had significant inverted U-shaped associations with doctoral research satisfaction. Moderate frequencies of use were associated with higher satisfaction, whereas excessively high frequencies were associated with lower satisfaction. Heterogeneity analysis indicated that the inverted U-shaped association held across STEM, medical and health, and humanities and social sciences disciplines, with the estimated peak being highest in STEM disciplines. AI efficiency perception showed a positive conditional instantaneous indirect effect in the association between AI use and research satisfaction, whereas AI risk perception showed a negative one. Overtime work pressure strengthened the quadratic associations between AI use and both AI efficiency perception and AI risk perception.

Large language models are accessible to a broad public and are increasingly used in advice-seeking contexts. In addition, artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools such as chatbots are also being implemented and tested in professional advisory settings. The present study investigates whether the evaluation of social relationships differs depending on whether users believe they are interacting with a human or an AI, and whether this effect varies across private vs. professional contexts. An online experiment with a 2 (AI vs. human) × 2 (private vs. professional) between-subjects design was conducted. Dependent variables included measures of perceived relationship quality, trust and epistemological beliefs towards AI. We found no significant effects of interaction partner nor context. However, participants’ epistemological beliefs about AI significantly predicted their evaluation of the AI counsellor. Specifically, two belief dimensions were relevant for the perceived relationship quality: justification and development. That is, the more integrative participants’ views on scientific knowledge acquisition in AI were, and the more they believed that knowledge evolves over time and is subject to revision, the more positively they evaluated the AI counsellor. Implications for the profession of social work are discussed: an understanding of AI and its influences on relationships are at the core of the profession.

documents.abstract: Maintaining up-to-date clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) is essential for evidence-based medicine (EBM), yet the current process is constrained by the rapid expansion of evidence and the complexity of expert consensus formation. To address this challenge, we developed GUIDE, a multi-agent copilot system that enables computationally augmented consensus for human-AI collaborative clinical guideline generation and updating, assigning labor-intensive tasks to specialized AI agents while preserving critical judgment and final arbitration for human experts. In a benchmark comprising 12 datasets derived from NICE ophthalmology-specific guidelines, GUIDE showed strong performance across evidence retrieval, assessment, and synthesis, achieving 88.85% literature recall, 86.06% alignment in certainty-of-evidence ratings, and 91.67% agreement on recommendations, only requiring 162.17 minutes per dataset on average (including 28.68% human intervention). Performance remained stable in additional 20 datasets spanning cardiology, endocrinology, gastroenterology, and respiratory medicine, indicating its cross-specialty generalizability. We then conducted an ablation analysis to validate the importance of human-AI collaboration mechanism, as removing expert intervention reduced performance in judgment-intensive steps such as Risk-of-Bias assessment. Furthermore, a simulated end-to-end evaluation using six post-cutoff datasets demonstrated that GUIDE maintained robust performance, supporting its ability to generalize to genuinely unseen evidence within a continuous guideline-updating workflow. Finally, prospective real-world validation in a live guideline updating process showed that GUIDE substantially alleviated expert workload across evidence selection, extraction, and synthesis. The GUIDE-assisted update was judged more clinically acceptable than the original guideline recommendation issued a decade earlier (mean score, 3.73 vs. 1.53; agreement, 66.7% vs. 13.3%) and achieved outcomes comparable to those of human-only updating (P = 0.588), while requiring substantially less time and expert effort. Together, our findings support GUIDE as a practical framework for timely, trustworthy, and expert-centric clinical guideline generation, and validate computationally augmented consensus as a feasible paradigm for enhanced guideline development.
