documents.abstract: Heuristic search has been a central paradigm of artificial intelligence since the earliest work on mechanised problem solving, and it remains embedded in automated planning, robot navigation, combinatorial optimisation, game playing and, increasingly, machine-learning systems that couple learned models with explicit search. Its literature, however, is divided among communities that rarely evaluate one another’s claims: optimal and bounded-suboptimal state-space search, constraint and satisfiability solving, local search and metaheuristics, adversarial and sampling-based search, and learning-based and language-model-based problem solving. This critical narrative review examines how heuristic knowledge is obtained, what guarantees it supports, how its performance is evidenced and where modern learning-based methods alter or leave intact the classical picture. Literature was identified through structured searches of multidisciplinary and discipline-specific scholarly indexes, supplemented by backward and forward citation tracing, with peer-reviewed journal articles and archival proceedings appraised for methodological adequacy, strength of baselines and transparency of computational reporting. The synthesis indicates that formal results on admissibility, consistency and node expansion remain the most secure part of the field, but their practical value depends on assumptions that learned and inadmissible heuristics frequently violate. Automatically derived heuristics from relaxation and abstraction are well supported in planning benchmarks, whereas learned heuristics show strong single-domain results and weaker, less consistent generalisation. Metaheuristic research combines genuinely effective problem-specific methods with a large volume of metaphor-driven proposals whose novelty and benchmarking practices have been seriously questioned. The most convincing recent advances integrate learned guidance with search and with external verification rather than replacing search altogether, while large language models appear more reliable as generators of candidate heuristics or code than as stand-alone planners. Unresolved questions concern generalisation across instance distributions, fair accounting of computational cost, robustness of learned guidance and reproducible evaluation. Progress is likely to depend less on new algorithmic metaphors than on shared benchmarks, stronger baselines and explicit reporting of what each method guarantees.

Homo Putans and the Politics of Algorithmic Futures: Prediction, Supposition, and Democratic Possibility This working paper examines how algorithmic prediction shapes political decision-making and the range of futures considered possible, credible, and worthy of democratic deliberation. It approaches this question through Homo Putans, the philosophical framework of the human being as a supposing being. Drawing on critical algorithm studies, artificial intelligence ethics, and democratic theory, the paper distinguishes prediction from supposition. Whereas algorithmic predictions estimate outcomes within particular data structures, models, and assumptions, supposition enables individuals and political communities to consider alternatives without requiring prior confidence in their probability or feasibility. Engaging with the work of Louise Amoore, Kate Crawford, Rob Kitchin, Abeba Birhane, and contemporary scholarship on algorithmic governance, the paper examines how computational predictions acquire institutional authority and influence political judgments. It proposes four interconnected analytical dimensions: target selection, institutional uptake, anticipatory adaptation, and evidential feedback. These dimensions help explain how algorithmic systems may shape not only decisions about possible futures but also the conditions under which those futures become politically conceivable. Building on the Homo Putans framework, the paper introduces the concept of a counter-suppositional audit, a normative approach to examining whether political alternatives excluded or marginalized by predictive systems can be reconsidered through democratic deliberation. The central argument is that algorithmic prediction should inform political judgment without determining the boundaries of democratic possibility. Even when computational systems provide valuable evidence, political communities must retain the capacity to question their assumptions, consider alternative futures, and revise decisions. By connecting the philosophy of supposition with debates on artificial intelligence, political imagination, and democratic accountability, the paper develops a conceptual perspective on the relationship between prediction, political authority, and the future of democratic agency. documents.abstract: Financial English teaching has long been beset by three persistent problems: students tend to understand terminology only superficially, their genre awareness remains weak, and they struggle to interpret data. Generative AI can offer cognitive scaffolding, but it also brings the risk of cognitive offloading, whereby students let the efficiency of the tool take the place of genuine cognitive engagement. Taking the Basic Financial English course in the Business English programme at an application-oriented university as a case, this study draws on distributed cognition and the notion of dual-teacher collaboration. Following the action research spiral proposed by Kemmis, it conducted three rounds of classroom interventions centred on human–AI collaboration. The first round employed a terminology cognitive conflict task to reposition AI; the second adopted reverse deconstruction of genre to establish boundaries in the human–AI division of labour; the third used correction of data narratives to develop critical human–AI collaboration literacy. Data from classroom observation, student reflective journals, AI dialogue logs and student work indicate that human–AI collaboration lowered the cognitive threshold of Financial English, but the quality of collaboration depended on whether the teacher could design structural tension between the efficiency that AI supplies and the cognitive retention that students achieve. The study identifies a progressive mechanism in human–AI collaboration, moving from cognitive offloading through cognitive conflict to cognitive retention, and discusses the conditions and limits under which it can be transferred to Financial English classrooms in application-oriented universities.

The delegation of professional judgment to artificial intelligence raises two questions that are especially pressing for professions built on documented judgment: which parts of expert work can be entrusted to algorithmic systems, and how can accountability be preserved when they are? This study examines these questions in external financial auditing, using journal entry testing (JET), a fraud-risk procedure that combines large-scale data screening with professional judgment, as a procedure-level case. A large language model (LLM) was instructed to screen a synthetic population of 1,000 journal entries against predefined risk indicators under a baseline prompt, a prompt to retain only items it was certain about, and a prompt to broaden the screen. An initial run was followed by six independent replication sessions and four sessions with paraphrased baseline prompts, with every flagged transaction exported for comparison. Repeating the identical baseline instruction produced near-identical selections (mean pairwise overlap 94.6%), and the fully specified weekend criterion returned the same count in every baseline, broadened and paraphrased session. Paraphrasing the instruction reduced overlap with the original selections to 87.1% on average, and paraphrased sessions overlapped with each other by 82.5%, whereas the certainty instruction produced unstable selections (51.9% overlap; 48 to 148 items retained). Where the instruction left a parameter open, the model resolved it sometimes consistently, as when it treated all pending and rejected entries as unapproved, and sometimes inconsistently, as with the jurisdiction of the holiday calendar or the window for period-end entries. The results suggest that in judgment-intensive screening, LLM output depends on how the request is framed and on interpretive choices that the instruction leaves to the model, with implications for documentation, review and accountability in AI-assisted professional work. The study does not assess fraud-detection accuracy; it offers a transparent, replicable design for locating where instruction-dependence enters an audit procedure.

documents.abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence is transforming not only how knowledge is produced but where ideas themselves originate. Historically, human ideation has been understood as an embodied process grounded in perception, cultural interpretation, and symbolic mediation. By tracing the genealogy of the concept of “idea” from its Indo-European roots linking seeing and knowing to its philosophical elaboration in Western thought, this paper shows how human thinking has traditionally been tied to sensory experience and culturally situated forms of interpretation. Generative AI introduces a fundamentally different procedure: ideas are produced through probabilistic recombination within large textual and symbolic archives rather than through perception or lived experience. Drawing on anthropological perspectives on culture and knowledge, the paper argues that generative systems do not reproduce a universal human culture but operate within stratified datasets that reflect historical asymmetries in language, power, and digital representation. As a result, the ideas emerging from these systems are shaped by synecdochic cultural environments in which statistically dominant perspectives come to stand for humanity as a whole. These dynamics become visible not only in discourse but also in technoscientific domains where generative models increasingly support hypothesis generation, molecular design, and materials discovery, including nanotechnological research. The paper concludes by examining the governance implications of this transformation. Contemporary intellectual property regimes assume that human subjects conceive ideas and subsequently express or implement them. However, when ideation emerges through recursive interaction between humans and generative systems, the traditional distinction between idea and expression becomes unstable. Building on recent legal scholarship, the article argues that the governance of innovation may need to reconsider where creative agency resides in hybrid cognitive ecologies. Rather than focusing exclusively on downstream artifacts, future regulatory frameworks must account for how ideas themselves are generated, distributed, and mediated within human–AI collaborations.

By analysing browsing history, past purchases, search behaviour, ratings, and demographic information, these systems suggest products that appear relevant to individual consumers. This paper reviews existing literature on the relationship between AI-based recommendation systems and consumer purchase intention in e-commerce. The review finds that recommendation quality, personalization, perceived usefulness, trust, and reduced search effort generally strengthen purchase intention. However, privacy concerns, perceived intrusiveness, algorithmic bias, and lack of transparency can reduce consumer acceptance. The paper concludes that AI recommendations can improve consumer engagement and sales conversion, but e-commerce firms must balance personalization with data privacy, explainability, and ethical data use

In this essay, I argue that the inclusion of marginalized knowers at the periphery of neoliberal business schools may be as pernicious as their exclusion. I show that epistemic marginalization persists because the forms of knowledge marginalized knowers seek to produce are situated within targeted lacunae, systematically produced, and actively maintained absences around particular bodies of knowledge. These lacunae constitute forbidden domains shaped by the normative structure of business schools and the interests of their powerful allies. Through this conceptualization, I argue that the margin is not an inferior outside to the center, but a structured absence constituted within it, necessary for the coherence and dominance of the center. In doing so, I challenge assumptions that meaningful dialogue between margin and center remains viable when the terms of engagement are already predetermined by the center itself. At the same time, through what I conceptualize as epistemic anchoring, I show that the persistence of marginalized bodies of knowledge depends not only, or even primarily, on engagement with the center, but on the construction and sustenance of alternative epistemic spaces and the ability of marginalized knowers to remain anchored within them.

documents.abstract: The rising digitalization of work risks eroding social proximity and the relational conditions that enable thriving through work. Against this background, we review literature on social proximity and identify a lack of theory explaining how feelings of interpersonal closeness emerge through social interactions at work. To address this gap, we develop interaction zones theory. We propose that the “social proximity zone” represents the intersection of two latent dimensions that we refer to as relational stakes and interactional ease, respectively. We use this two-by-two framework to characterize interactional experiences, building on the circumplex model of affect as a foundation. A central proposition is that repeated and shared interactions in the social proximity zone contribute to individual and team thriving, based on the assumption that thriving requires interactions that are sufficiently challenging to enable learning yet flow with sufficient ease to ensure vitality. Finally, we argue that the social proximity zone can be purposively designed by creating relational stakes (e.g., through individual job design) and facilitating interactional ease (e.g., through team design). We outline a multilevel research agenda, calling for renewed attention to the importance of human-to-human interaction for individual thriving, team effectiveness, and broader organizational capabilities.

The physical and cognitive behavior of humans working in manufacturing environments is an issue that is becoming increasingly important with the advent of Industry 5.0. In this context, monitoring operators is fundamental to provide the situational awareness required for safe and dynamic robot control policies. In fact, to guarantee the well-being of human workers, collaborative robots must continuously adapt their control loops based on the operator’s actions, thereby reducing risky situations. In this work, the HA4M dataset is used to empirically assess human action recognition (HAR) in a manufacturing environment, acting as a perceptual system for Human–Robot Collaboration (HRC). This study introduces a framework for the on-site calibration of deep learning models to a specific subject, providing highly tailored feedback for the robot’s control architecture. Specifically, the study focuses on training two deep learning architectures, namely MS-TCN++ and LTContext, on RGB data to allow such models to properly adjust to a specific subject. Features are extracted using the inflated 3D model and arranged in matrix-wise and array-wise dimensions to evaluate the impact of data formatting. A ten-stage iterative boosting training strategy is implemented to systematically analyze model refinement by focusing on misclassified samples. It has been proven that the iterative framework drastically reduces the computational overhead, cutting the training time from 64 to 25 h for the MS-TCN++ and from 11 to just 5 h for the LTContext. In addition to such massive time savings, both networks maintain robust classification performance. Such results highlight the comprehensive engineering advantages of the proposed pipeline, laying the foundation for tightly coupled human-in-the-loop control strategies where robots can accurately perceive and preemptively react to operator actions.

Job uncertainty is one of the challenges facing the younger generation in Indonesia. Job competition, technological advancements, and job instability can affect motivation and psychological readiness for the professional world. This article discusses the impact of job uncertainty on motivation, stress, and the psychological well-being of the younger generation through a literature review. The results of the study indicate that job uncertainty can increase anxiety, decrease motivation, and affect self-confidence. Therefore, skills, adaptability, and mental preparedness are important factors in coping with changes in the world of work. Keywords: Job uncertainty, younger generation, motivation, psychological preparedness. Introduction Changes in the Indonesian workforce present both opportunities and challenges for the younger generation. Increasingly fierce job competition, technological advancements, and shifting industry needs have made securing stable employment a major concern. This uncertainty not only affects economic conditions but can also impact individuals’ psychological well-being. (Sitinjak, 2025) explains that young workers in Indonesia face various psychological challenges, such as stress, burnout, job insecurity, and a decline in motivation in the digital workplace. Therefore, readiness for the workforce must be assessed not only in terms of academic abilities and skills, but also in terms of mental preparedness to cope with uncertainty. Impact on Motivation and Psychological Readiness Job uncertainty can affect the younger generation’s motivation to plan and develop their careers. When job opportunities seem limited, individuals may lose confidence and feel that their efforts may not yield the desired results. According to (Sitinjak, 2025), intrinsic motivation, flexibility, and meaningful work are important factors for young workers. However, motivation can decline when the work environment is unsupportive and an individual’s psychological needs are not met. In addition to motivation, job uncertainty can also cause stress and anxiety. Research (Mboeik, 2026) found a significant negative correlation between stress levels and psychological well-being among workers who had been laid off. This suggests that the stress resulting from job loss can affect a person’s mental health. Thus, job insecurity can pose a challenge for the younger generation, particularly in building self-confidence, setting career goals, and preparing for the professional world. Strategies for Coping with Job Market Uncertainty To cope with these conditions, the younger generation needs to prepare themselves in several ways. First, they should improve skills that align with industry needs, particularly digital and communication skills. Second, they should build self-confidence and motivation to continue learning and growing. Third, they should develop stress management skills through positive activities and social support. (Azmi, 2025)explains that coping strategies such as managing information, limiting exposure to negative information, and sharing feelings with trusted individuals can help individuals cope with the psychological stress caused by uncertainty. In addition, companies and educational institutions also play a role in supporting the younger generation’s resilience through skills training, career development, and environments that foster psychological well-being. Conclusion Job market uncertainty in Indonesia is not only an economic challenge but can also affect the motivation and psychological readiness of the younger generation. Stress, anxiety, and declining self-confidence are some of the impacts that need to be addressed. Therefore, the younger generation needs to build their readiness by improving their skills, motivation, adaptability, and stress management. With strong professional and psychological readiness, the younger generation is expected to be able to face changes in the workplace with greater confidence.

Introduction Against the backdrop of widespread artificial intelligence (AI) integration in organizational settings, this study draws on the Job Demands-Resources model and categorization theory to examine the association between job skill demand and employee thriving at work and its underlying psychological mechanisms, with a focus on the dual mediating roles of AI opportunity perception and AI threat perception, and the moderating effect of approach motivation. Methods A progressive two-study design was adopted with two independent two-wave time-lagged samples of Chinese employees (Study 1: N = 298; Study 2: N = 301). Study 1 preliminarily tested the core main effects, and study 2 replicated the findings and further verified the mediating and moderating mechanisms using hierarchical regression and the PROCESS macro. Results Job skill demand positively predicts AI opportunity perception and negatively predicts AI threat perception. Both opportunity and threat perceptions significantly mediate the relationship between job skill demand and thriving at work. Furthermore, approach motivation significantly moderates the first-stage relationships: it strengthens the positive association between job skill demand and AI opportunity perception and amplifies the negative association between job skill demand and AI threat perception. However, the overall moderated mediation effect does not reach conventional statistical significance. Discussion These findings extend the application of the JD-R model in AI-enabled work contexts and provide practical insights for organizational AI transformation and employee work well-being promotion.

This conceptual-pedagogical article examines how conversational generative artificial intelligence can be incorporated into the teaching and learning of ethnography without weakening its situated, relational, and ethical foundations. It offers a selective conceptual synthesis rather than a systematic review or empirical evaluation: the proposed model is an implementable pedagogical design derived from recent debates on AI in anthropology, synthetic ethnography, synthetic interlocutors, LLM-generated social science data, and ethnographic pedagogy. The article argues that AI should be treated as a device for rehearsal, comparison, critique, and methodological reflection, not as a source of empirical authority. The model is organized around six formative moments: preparation before the field, AI-based rehearsal, peer role-play, non-delegable field encounter, post-field analysis and writing, and evaluation with mandatory revision. Across these moments, the activities are designed to support students’ ethnographic judgment through unaided attempts, instructor scaffolding, comparison with AI-generated outputs, structured debriefing, traceability to field materials, and justified revision. The article also refines the concept of false ethnography, understood not as synthetic text per se, but as false provenance, unwarranted empirical attribution, and lack of accountability to interlocutors. It concludes that generative AI may generate analytical inputs and pedagogical contrasts, but ethnographic claims remain authorized only through situated evidence, ethical responsibility, relational accountability to interlocutors, and critically audited documentation that supports but does not replace such accountability.

documents.abstract: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), AI dependence has become a growing concern in higher education. The present longitudinal study examined the associations between AI dependence and three components of school engagement (cognitive, emotional, and behavioral) among university students, as well as the moderating role of gender. The sample comprised 961 students from two universities in southern China who completed self-reported measures at two time points six months apart. After controlling for baseline engagement levels, higher AI dependence at Time 1 was significantly associated with lower cognitive, emotional, and behavioral engagement six months later. Gender did not moderate the association between AI dependence and cognitive engagement. However, gender moderation was significant for emotional and behavioral engagement. Specifically, the negative association with emotional engagement was significant only for female students, whereas the negative association with behavioral engagement was stronger for male students. AI dependence was measured only at Time 1, so the findings are prospective associations rather than causal effects, and reverse causality cannot be ruled out. These findings reveal distinct gender-differentiated patterns across engagement components and offer tentative practical implications for the prevention and intervention of university students’ school engagement in the AI era. These findings are primarily applicable to students with backgrounds similar to those in the present sample, and future research is needed to determine their generalizability to other populations.

documents.abstract: The International Safety Management Code places safety-management systems at the center of shipping safety, yet casualty investigations show that procedures, information, and responsibilities can exist without an effective risk control. To examine where artificial intelligence (AI) might assist, two coders independently classified 53 investigator-established safety-management factors in 14 final reports from five authorities. We adjudicated their assignments against the reports. Procedural decoupling was the most frequent mechanism (21 factors), and relevant structured or unstructured information existed for 43. Under our qualitative sufficiency rule, 48 primary interventions were procedural or organizational and five were engineering or deterministic. The coders identified potential advisory AI roles for 11 and 33 factors, with 18 after adjudication. No factor was assigned a consequential AI authority in this retrospective analysis. With all six intervention classes available, a maritime practitioner independently selected non-AI primary controls for all 20 sampled factors. In four reports, adding eight distinct factors identified by practitioners increased advisory assignments from 4 of 16 to 8 of 24. We propose Observability, Actionability, and Governability as the qualitative decision architecture for assessing whether a safety-relevant condition can be observed, whether a feasible response has an accountable owner, and whether an additional AI role can be governed.

Artificial intelligence has rapidly become embedded in everyday cognitive tasks, transforming how individuals access, digest, and rely on information. This transformation shifts cognitive effort from internal memory to external systems, raising critical questions about how sustained interaction with AI systems is reshaping the mechanisms of human memory. To examine these effects, in this paper, evidence from cognitive neuroscience and behavioral studies was integrated to ultimately analyze how AI-controlled environments alter encoding and retrieval processes. Experimental and correlational findings were used to evaluate how factors such as attention, emotional relevance, and retrieval methods shape memory retention and cognitive offloading patterns. Results indicate that AI does not reduce memory capacity, but redistributes cognitive effort, selectively externalizing low-relevance information while preserving meaningful knowledge internally. There is, however, a downstream association to changes in critical thinking. These findings suggest that AI contributes to a hybrid memory system, redefining memory as a distributed process across biological and technological systems, with new developing mechanisms for long-term cognitive development.

This article examines the methodology of creating a virtual classroom environment using artificial intelligence (AI) agents in pedagogical higher education institutions and its use in training future teachers. The article analyzes the structural components of the virtual classroom environment, the capabilities of AI agents operating in various roles (student, parent, administrator), and their effectiveness in preparing for pedagogical practice. The research results show that the AI-based virtual classroom environment significantly improves the quality of studentsʻ pre-practice preparation.

The methodology is being piloted within the educational compo­nents "Fundamentals of Scientific Research and Organization of Science" and "Patent Law and Copyright." Permissible methods for applying AI, as well as the risks and limitations associated with its use in the educational process, are defined.

documents.abstract: Motion graphics is a hybrid audiovisual language. It developed between graphic design, cinema and animation, and it has its own grammar of moving typography, layers and rhythm. This conceptual analysis studies how generative artificial intelligence (AI), especially diffusion models for image and video, changes this language and the idea of authorship in the field. The article starts from the history of motion design, from Saul Bass and John Whitney to Kyle Cooper. It then connects this history with recent research on AI images, creativity and creative work. The article identifies three main changes in audiovisual language. First, the design process moves from building an image step by step to describing it with a text prompt. Second, a new visual style appears, based on fluid transformations and on the most common patterns in the training data, with a risk of similar results for everybody. Third, realistic AI images change how viewers trust what they see. These changes are structural and do not depend on the current technical limits of the tools. In relation to authorship, the designer moves from creating forms to choosing, directing and editing what the machine produces. Authorship becomes a process in layers, where intention, documentation and style are key. Current law also places authorship in these human decisions, in the United States and the European Union and, with different thresholds, in Asian jurisdictions such as China, Japan and South Korea. The article also discusses how studios can keep training young designers when AI automates entry-level tasks. It proposes a simple framework with four dimensions of change and three modes of human–machine authorship. The aim is to support research, professional practice and education in motion design.

The study examines the applicability of self-determination theory (SDT) in understanding student engagement in physical and metaverse-based classrooms. The psychological demands of autonomy, relatedness, and competence, as defined by SDT, have been examined in traditional or physical classrooms, but their relevance in the metaverse classroom remains unexplored. To address this gap, we conducted a comparative survey among MBA students attending both physical and metaverse classes. Our findings reveal differences in how the SDT-based psychological needs influence the agentic, behavioral, cognitive, and emotional engagement across physical and metaverse classes. Our results challenge the assumption that SDT applies uniformly across contexts, providing new insights into how motivation-related constructs function in digital learning environments. The study contributes to the literature on digital education, highlighting the need to adapt motivational theories to the metaverse classroom.

Organizations’ use of cognitive automation technologies, from simple rule-based systems to more advanced machine learning and large language models, to enhance knowledge-intensive work is on the rise. However, the impact of these systems on employee skills is becoming a growing concern. How does cognitive automation transform existing work, roles, and expertise? What happens to professional skills if employees rely heavily on automation? The teaching case delves into these questions in the context of accounting, a specialist field wherein several types of cognitive automation are being deployed. This domain – amenable to digital processing and automation because of its immaterial nature – provides an illuminating backdrop for considering the trade-offs between maintaining expertise and enhancing efficiency. The case can serve undergraduate or more advanced information systems or accounting courses.

Objective of the study: To analyze how the integration of Knowledge Management (KM), Absorptive Capacity (ACAP), and Sociotechnical Dynamics (SD) influences the governance and efficiency of Innovation-Promoting Environments (IPEs). Methodology/approach: A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted informed by the PRISMA 2020 statement. We analyzed 61 peer-reviewed articles using descriptive profiling of the corpus, a term co-occurrence analysis in VOSviewer and inductive thematic synthesis to map articulation patterns. Originality/Relevance: The study addresses the "productivity paradox" in ecosystems, filling the theoretical gap on how physical/digital infrastructures (SD) align with the cognitive capabilities (ACAP) of tenant firms, utilizing a Paradox Theory lens. Main results: We identified four distinct articulation patterns (Recursive, Linear-Mediated, Systemic, and Emergent) and three constitutive paradoxes (e.g., Openness vs. Appropriation) that shape ecosystem evolution. Theoretical/methodological contributions: The study proposes a novel multilevel framework bridging engineering (systems) and strategic management perspectives, arguing that IPE success depends on a meta-capability to navigate tensions rather than solving them. Social/management contributions: The framework offers ecosystem orchestrators and policymakers a diagnostic tool to align infrastructure investments with organizational capabilities, preventing "empty shell" ecosystems.
